Guide to the transcription¶

Use this page for the full derivation behind Lecture 7: polynomial coordinates, integrated derivative basis and Runge-Kutta equations, continuity and counting, time scaling and implementation, and sparse structure.

The existing quadrature implementation below remains useful for experiments. The orthogonality proof is taught in the numerical-integration lecture and developed in Numeric Integration for DAEs. For exact coefficient construction, see Collocation Points and Runge-Kutta Coefficients; for a solved model, see Pyomo.DAE Example: Race Car.

Primary sources: Biegler (2010), Chapter 8, p. 216, and Chapter 10, pp. 289–298, with the Chapter 10 errata; Ascher & Petzold (1998), Section 4.7, pp. 101–104.

We now turn a DAE-constrained dynamic optimization problem into a sparse nonlinear program. We approximate state and control profiles with piecewise polynomials and enforce the DAE at collocation points. This simultaneous, or direct-transcription, approach is closely related to the implicit Runge--Kutta methods developed in the numerical-integration lecture.

Quadrature Methods¶

We begin with the quadrature ideas needed to derive collocation. The next notebooks apply the method to dynamic optimization examples. For more detail, see:

  • Chapter 9 in Biegler (2010)

  • Chapter 16, Gauss Quadrature and Multi-dimensional Integrals, in McClarren (2018)

Main Idea¶

The quadrature rule approximates the integral III with weighted sum of function evaluations:

I:=∫−11f(x)dx≈∑l=1Lwlf(xl)⏟quadrature ruleI := \int_{-1}^{1} f(x) dx \approx \underbrace{\sum_{l=1}^{L} w_l f(x_l)}_{\text{quadrature rule}}I:=∫−11​f(x)dx≈quadrature rulel=1∑L​wl​f(xl​)​​

where:

  • xlx_lxl​ are nodes (also known as abscissas)

  • wlw_lwl​ are weights

  • LLL number of nodes and weights

Central questions:

  • How to choose nodes and weights?

  • How does this choice impact approximation error?

  • How does LLL impact approximation error?

Polynomial degree and coefficient count¶

A polynomial p(t)=∑j=0Kajtjp(t)=\sum_{j=0}^K a_jt^jp(t)=∑j=0K​aj​tj has K+1K+1K+1 coefficients and degree at most KKK, with equality when aK≠0a_K\ne0aK​=0. Some older texts call that polynomial “order K+1K+1K+1.” Here degree denotes the highest power; order denotes the rate at which a numerical error decreases.

Gauss-Legendre quadrature¶

With the Gauss-Legendre nodes and weights, the LLL-point rule is exact for every polynomial of degree at most 2L−12L-12L−1. No LLL-node rule with real nodes can be exact through degree 2L2L2L: the squared node polynomial ∏l(x−xl)2\prod_l(x-x_l)^2∏l​(x−xl​)2 is zero at all nodes but has a positive integral. This is optimal polynomial exactness, rather than a claim of minimum error for every nonpolynomial integrand.

Why 2L−12L-12L−1?¶

Let f(x)=a2L−1x2L−1+a2L−2x2L−2+...+a1x1+a0f(x) = a_{2L-1} x^{2L-1} + a_{2L-2} x^{2L-2} + ... + a_{1} x^1 + a_{0}f(x)=a2L−1​x2L−1+a2L−2​x2L−2+...+a1​x1+a0​

Exactness through degree 2L−12L-12L−1 imposes 2L2L2L moment equations (one for each monomial 1,x,…,x2L−11,x,\ldots,x^{2L-1}1,x,…,x2L−1). These match the 2L2L2L unknown node and weight values in an LLL-point rule. This count motivates the attainable degree; orthogonal-polynomial theory supplies the nodes and proves exactness.

How to determine the nodes and weights?¶

One way to derive the Gauss-Legendre quadrature rules is by looking at the integral generic monomials of degree 0 up to 2L−12L-12L−1 and setting each equal to the LLL point Gauss-Legendre quadrature rule:

∫−11dx a0x0=a0∑l=1Lwlxl0,∫−11dx a1x1=a1∑l=1Lwlxl1,  ⋮∫−11dx a2L−1x2L−1=a2L−1∑l=1Lwlxl2L−1.\begin{align*} \int\limits_{-1}^{1} dx\, a_0 x^0 &= a_0\sum_{l=1}^L w_l x_l^0, \\ \int\limits_{-1}^{1} dx\, a_1 x^1 &= a_1\sum_{l=1}^L w_l x_l^1, \\ & ~~ \vdots \\ \int\limits_{-1}^{1} dx\, a_{2L-1} x^{2L-1} &= a_{2L-1}\sum_{l=1}^L w_l x_l^{2L-1}. \end{align*}−1∫1​dxa0​x0−1∫1​dxa1​x1−1∫1​dxa2L−1​x2L−1​=a0​l=1∑L​wl​xl0​,=a1​l=1∑L​wl​xl1​,  ⋮=a2L−1​l=1∑L​wl​xl2L−1​.​
(1)

Notice that the aia_iai​ constants cancel out of each equation so they do not matter. This system is 2L2L2L equations with LLL weights, wlw_lwl​, and LLL nodes, xlx_lxl​. We could solve these equations to get the weights and nodes, though this is not how it is done in practice generally---this is accomplished by using the theory of orthogonal polynomials.

Code¶

def GLQuad(f, L=8, dataReturn=False):
    """Compute the Gauss-Legendre Quadrature estimate
    of the integral of f(x) from -1 to 1
    Inputs:
    f:   name of function to integrate
    L:   Number of quadrature nodes. Tabulated here for L <= 8;
         larger L falls through to numpy.polynomial.legendre.leggauss.
    dataReturn:   determines whether weights and xs are returned

    Returns:
    G-L Quadrature estimate"""

    # Set bound on L
    assert L >= 1

    # Enumerate over L to define weights and x in each scenario
    if L == 1:
        weights = np.ones(1) * 2
        xs = np.array([0])
    elif L == 2:
        weights = np.ones(2)
        xs = np.array([-np.sqrt(1.0 / 3.0), np.sqrt(1.0 / 3.0)])

            [
                0.8888888888888888888888889,

        )
        xs = np.array([0.0, -0.7745966692414833770358531, 0.7745966692414833770358531])

    # Calculate the quadrature estimate
    quad_estimate = np.sum(weights * f(xs))

    if dataReturn:
        return quad_estimate, weights, xs
    else:
        return quad_estimate

Polynomial Example¶

As a simple demonstration of the Gauss-Legendre quadrature, let’s show that it integrates polynomials of degree 2L−12L-12L−1 exactly. Consider the integral

∫−11(x+1)2L−1 dx=22L−1L.\int\limits_{-1}^1 (x+1)^{2L-1}\,dx = \frac{2^{2 L-1}}{L}.−1∫1​(x+1)2L−1dx=L22L−1​.
(2)

We can use the GLQuad function to evaluate the error.

L = np.arange(1, 12)
for l in L:

    # Create f
    f = lambda x: (x + 1) ** (2 * l - 1)

    # Evaluate exact (analytic) solution
    integral = 2 ** (2 * l - 1) / l

    # Evaluate quadrature rule
    GLintegral = GLQuad(f, l)

    # Print results
    print(
        "L =",
        l,
        "\t Estimate is",
        GLintegral,
        "Exact value is",
        integral,
        "\nAbs. Relative Error is",
        np.abs(GLintegral - integral) / integral,
    )

Generalization¶

We are generally interested in integrals not just over the domain x∈[−1,1]x\in [-1,1]x∈[−1,1]. We’ll now make a function that does Gauss-Legendre quadrature over a general range using the formula

∫abf(x) dx=b−a2∫−11f(b−a2z+a+b2) dz.\int_a^b f(x)\,dx = \frac{b-a}{2} \int_{-1}^1 f\left(\frac{b-a}{2}z + \frac{a+b}{2}\right)\,dz.∫ab​f(x)dx=2b−a​∫−11​f(2b−a​z+2a+b​)dz.
(3)
def generalGL(f, a, b, L):
    """Compute the Gauss-Legendre Quadrature estimate
    of the integral of f(x) from a to b
    Inputs:
    f:   name of function to integrate
    a:   lower bound of integral
    b:   upper bound of integral
    L:   Number of quadrature nodes (see GLQuad)
    Returns:
    G-L Quadrature estimate"""

    # Set bound on L
    assert L >= 1

    # Define a re-scaled f
    f_rescaled = lambda z: f(0.5 * (b - a) * z + 0.5 * (a + b))

    # Define the integral
    integral = GLQuad(f_rescaled, L)

    # Calculate the G-L quadrature estimate
    return integral * (b - a) * 0.5

Let’s show that this version integrates polynomials of degree 2L−12L-12L−1 exactly. Consider the integral

∫−32(x+1)2L−1 dx=9L−4L2L.\int\limits_{-3}^2 (x+1)^{2L-1}\,dx = \frac{9^L-4^L}{2 L}.−3∫2​(x+1)2L−1dx=2L9L−4L​.
(4)
L = np.arange(1, 12)

# Loop over L to calculate the integral and the G-L estimate
for l in L:
    # Define a lambda function
    f = lambda x: (x + 1) ** (2 * l - 1)
    # Calculate the integral
    integral = (9**l - 4**l) / (2 * l)
    # Calculate the estimate
    GLintegral = generalGL(f, -3, 2, l)
    # Print statement for the error comparison
    print(
        "L =",
        l,
        "\t Estimate is",
        GLintegral,
        "Exact value is",
        integral,
        "\nAbs. Relative Error is",
        np.abs(GLintegral - integral) / integral,
    )

Radau Quadrature¶

Sometimes we desire either:

  • The first node is at the beginning of the interval, i.e., x1=−1x_1 = -1x1​=−1 or

  • The last node is at the end of the interval, i.e., xL=1x_{L} = 1xL​=1.

This is known as Gauss-Radau quadrature. The remaining nodes and weights are chosen optimally; thus, Radau quadrature exactly integrates all polynomials of degree 2L−22L-22L−2 or less. Specifying one of the nodes leaves only 2L−12L-12L−1 degrees of freedom.

More info: https://mathworld.wolfram.com/RadauQuadrature.html

Differential Equations¶

Consider solving the differential equation

x˙=f(t,x),x(t0)=x0,\dot{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{f}(t,\mathbf{x}), \quad \mathbf{x}(t_0) = \mathbf{x}_0,x˙=f(t,x),x(t0​)=x0​,
(5)

to determine x(tf)\mathbf{x}(t_f)x(tf​). This can be expressed as an integral:

x(tf)=∫t0tfdxdtdt+x0=∫t0tff(t,x(t))dt⏟quadrature rule+x0\mathbf{x}(t_f) = \int_{t_0}^{t_f} \frac{d\mathbf{x}}{dt} dt + \mathbf{x}_0 = \underbrace{\int_{t_0}^{t_f} \mathbf{f}(t, \mathbf{x}(t)) dt}_{\text{quadrature rule}} + \mathbf{x}_0x(tf​)=∫t0​tf​​dtdx​dt+x0​=quadrature rule∫t0​tf​​f(t,x(t))dt​​+x0​
(6)

Thus, Runge-Kutta methods can be interpreted as a quadrature rule.

Collocation Methods¶

See the following resources for more information on collocation:

  • Chapter 10 in Biegler (2010)

What is a Collocation Method?¶

https://encyclopediaofmath.org/wiki/Collocation_method

A collocation method approximates the state with a polynomial and enforces the differential and algebraic equations at selected collocation points. The resulting finite system of algebraic equations can be solved directly or embedded in an optimization problem.

Derivation of Collocation Methods¶

Derivations are followed from Section 10.2 of Biegler (2010).

Consider the following multiperiod dynamic optimization problem (8.5).

min⁡∑l=1NTΦl(zl(tl),yl(tl),ul(tl),pl) s.t. dzldt=fl(zl(t),yl(t),ul(t),pl),zl(tl−1)=z0l,gl(zl(t),yl(t),ul(t),pl)=0,uLl≤ul(t)≤uUl,pLl≤pl≤pUl,yLl≤yl(t)≤yUl,zLl≤zl(t)≤zUl,t∈(tl−1,tl],l=1,…,NT,h(p,z01,z1(t1),z02,z2(t2),…,z0NT,zNT(tNT))=0\begin{align*} \min & \sum_{l=1}^{N_T} \Phi^l\left(\mathbf{z}^l\left(t_l\right), \mathbf{y}^l\left(t_l\right), \mathbf{u}^l\left(t_l\right), \mathbf{p}^l\right) \\ \text { s.t. } & \frac{d \mathbf{z}^l}{d t}=\mathbf{f}^l\left(\mathbf{z}^l(t), \mathbf{y}^l(t), \mathbf{u}^l(t), \mathbf{p}^l\right), \quad \mathbf{z}^l\left(t_{l-1}\right)=\mathbf{z}_0^l, \\ & \mathbf{g}^l\left(\mathbf{z}^l(t), \mathbf{y}^l(t), \mathbf{u}^l(t), \mathbf{p}^l\right)=\mathbf{0}, \\ & \mathbf{u}_L^l \leq \mathbf{u}^l(t) \leq \mathbf{u}_U^l, \\ & \mathbf{p}_L^l \leq \mathbf{p}^l \leq \mathbf{p}_U^l, \\ & \mathbf{y}_L^l \leq \mathbf{y}^l(t) \leq \mathbf{y}_U^l, \\ & \mathbf{z}_L^l \leq \mathbf{z}^l(t) \leq \mathbf{z}_U^l, \quad t \in\left(t_{l-1}, t_l\right], l=1, \ldots, N_T, \\ & \mathbf{h}\left(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{z}_0^1, \mathbf{z}^1\left(t_1\right), \mathbf{z}_0^2, \mathbf{z}^2\left(t_2\right), \ldots, \mathbf{z}_0^{N_T}, \mathbf{z}^{N_T}\left(t_{N_T}\right)\right)=\mathbf{0} \end{align*}min s.t. ​l=1∑NT​​Φl(zl(tl​),yl(tl​),ul(tl​),pl)dtdzl​=fl(zl(t),yl(t),ul(t),pl),zl(tl−1​)=z0l​,gl(zl(t),yl(t),ul(t),pl)=0,uLl​≤ul(t)≤uUl​,pLl​≤pl≤pUl​,yLl​≤yl(t)≤yUl​,zLl​≤zl(t)≤zUl​,t∈(tl−1​,tl​],l=1,…,NT​,h(p,z01​,z1(t1​),z02​,z2(t2​),…,z0NT​​,zNT​(tNT​​))=0​
(7)

Each physical period lll may contain many finite elements. Period junctions use the coupling function h\mathbf hh; finite-element boundaries within a period use state continuity. The decision variables include the nodal states, control coefficients and any free parameters. A running cost can be included by adding an accumulator state, q˙=L(z,y,u,p,t)\dot q=L(\mathbf z,\mathbf y,\mathbf u,\mathbf p,t)q˙​=L(z,y,u,p,t), and minimizing q(tf)q(t_f)q(tf​) plus terminal cost.

State coordinates on one element¶

The collocation method can be developed by solving the differential equation (dz/dt dz/dt dz/dt) at specific time points. For example, Figure 10.1 shows the state variable approximation for a single finite element:

zK(t)=α0+α1t+⋯+αKtK\begin{align} \mathbf{z}^K(t) = \boldsymbol\alpha_0 + \boldsymbol\alpha_1t + \cdots + \boldsymbol\alpha_Kt^K \end{align}zK(t)=α0​+α1​t+⋯+αK​tK​​
(8)

The coefficients αj\boldsymbol\alpha_jαj​ are vectors when the state is a vector. A power basis is mathematically valid, but nodal Lagrange coefficients are directly interpretable as state values. This profile can also be represented as a Lagrange interpolation polynomial. For Gauss-Legendre or right Radau, choose K+1K+1K+1 distinct interpolation points within element iii, the state can be represented as:

t=ti−1+hiτ,zK(t)=∑j=0Kℓj(τ)zij,for t∈[ti−1,ti] and τ∈[0,1],where ℓj(τ)=∏k=0k≠jK(τ−τk)(τj−τk)τ0=0τj<τj+1,j=0,...,K−1,and hi is the length of element i.\begin{align} & t = t_{i-1} + h_i\tau , \\ & \mathbf{z}^K(t) = \sum_{j=0}^K \ell_j(\tau)\mathbf{z}_{ij} , \\ & \text{for } t \in [t_{i-1},t_i] \text{ and } \tau \in [0,1] , \\ & \text{where } \ell_j(\tau) = \prod_{\substack{k=0 \\ k\neq j}}^K \frac{(\tau-\tau_k)}{(\tau_j-\tau_k)} \\ & \tau_0=0 \\ & \tau_j<\tau_{j+1}, \\ & j=0,...,K-1 , \\ & \text{and } h_i \text{ is the length of element } i. \\ \end{align}​t=ti−1​+hi​τ,zK(t)=j=0∑K​ℓj​(τ)zij​,for t∈[ti−1​,ti​] and τ∈[0,1],where ℓj​(τ)=k=0k=j​∏K​(τj​−τk​)(τ−τk​)​τ0​=0τj​<τj+1​,j=0,...,K−1,and hi​ is the length of element i.​​
(9)

The key property of this polynomial is that zK(tij)=zij z^K(t_{ij})=z_{ij} zK(tij​)=zij​ where tij=ti−1+τjhi t_{ij}=t_{i-1} + \tau_j h_i tij​=ti−1​+τj​hi​.

At τ=τk\tau=\tau_kτ=τk​, every ℓj\ell_jℓj​ with j≠kj\ne kj=k contains a zero numerator; ℓk(τk)=1\ell_k(\tau_k)=1ℓk​(τk​)=1. Thus zK(tik)=zik\mathbf z^K(t_{ik})=\mathbf z_{ik}zK(tik​)=zik​. The basis also satisfies ∑jℓj=1\sum_j\ell_j=1∑j​ℓj​=1: both sides interpolate the constant polynomial at K+1K+1K+1 distinct nodes. These identities justify interpreting coefficients as nodal values.

Why change coordinates? Power coefficients are not nodal states, so componentwise bounds on those coefficients do not directly impose physical state bounds. Monomial Vandermonde systems can also become poorly conditioned as the degree grows or the time interval is badly scaled; nearly dependent columns make coefficients sensitive even when the represented profile changes little. Normalizing each element and using nodal coordinates makes the variables easier to interpret. It does not remove every conditioning problem, and nodal bounds still need the between-node check below.

Bounds are nodal. Imposing zL≤zij≤zU\mathbf z_L\le\mathbf z_{ij}\le\mathbf z_UzL​≤zij​≤zU​ does not bound the whole polynomial. Lagrange basis functions can be negative between nodes. Check additional points, extrema of the interpolation polynomial, or the independently integrated trajectory. For a continuous path constraint, mesh refinement and a residual check are part of validation.

The counterexample below uses p(τ)=4.2τ(1−τ)p(\tau)=4.2\tau(1-\tau)p(τ)=4.2τ(1−τ) at the initial point and three right-Radau nodes. Every nodal value lies in [0,1][0,1][0,1], but p(1/2)=1.05p(1/2)=1.05p(1/2)=1.05.

radau = np.array([(4-np.sqrt(6))/10,(4+np.sqrt(6))/10,1.0])
nodes = np.r_[0.0,radau]
values = 4.2*nodes*(1-nodes)
assert np.all((values>=0)&(values<=1))
assert np.isclose(4.2*0.5*(1-0.5),1.05)
print("Nodal values:",values,"; value at tau=1/2:",1.05)
Nodal values: [0.         0.55024286 0.96175714 0.        ] ; value at tau=1/2: 1.05

Integrated derivative basis gives Runge-Kutta equations¶

Let KKK distinct derivative nodes be cjc_jcj​. Define

ℓˉj(τ)=∏k≠jτ−ckcj−ck,Ωj(τ)=∫0τℓˉj(s) ds.\bar\ell_j(\tau)=\prod_{k\ne j}\frac{\tau-c_k}{c_j-c_k},\qquad \Omega_j(\tau)=\int_0^\tau\bar\ell_j(s)\,ds.ℓˉj​(τ)=k=j∏​cj​−ck​τ−ck​​,Ωj​(τ)=∫0τ​ℓˉj​(s)ds.
(10)

The derivative polynomial has degree at most K−1K-1K−1; integrating it with the initial value gives

zK(ti−1+hiτ)=zi−1+hi∑k=1KΩk(τ)vik.\mathbf z^K(t_{i-1}+h_i\tau)=\mathbf z_{i-1}+h_i\sum_{k=1}^K\Omega_k(\tau)\mathbf v_{ik}.zK(ti−1​+hi​τ)=zi−1​+hi​k=1∑K​Ωk​(τ)vik​.
(11)

Here vik\mathbf v_{ik}vik​ denotes the physical-time derivative, not the state. Differentiating cancels the factor hih_ihi​, and ℓˉk(cj)=δkj\bar\ell_k(c_j)=\delta_{kj}ℓˉk​(cj​)=δkj​ gives dzK/dt(tij)=vijd\mathbf z^K/dt(t_{ij})=\mathbf v_{ij}dzK/dt(tij​)=vij​. The factor arises from dt=hi dτdt=h_i\,d\taudt=hi​dτ.

For a semi-explicit DAE, enforce

vij=f(Zij,Yij,Uij,p,tij),0=g(Zij,Yij,Uij,p,tij).\mathbf v_{ij}=\mathbf f(\mathbf Z_{ij},\mathbf Y_{ij},\mathbf U_{ij},\mathbf p,t_{ij}),\qquad \mathbf0=\mathbf g(\mathbf Z_{ij},\mathbf Y_{ij},\mathbf U_{ij},\mathbf p,t_{ij}).vij​=f(Zij​,Yij​,Uij​,p,tij​),0=g(Zij​,Yij​,Uij​,p,tij​).
(12)

Evaluating the state at the stages and endpoint gives

Zij=zi−1+hi∑kajkfik,ajk=Ωk(cj),zi=zi−1+hi∑kbkfik,bk=Ωk(1).\begin{aligned} \mathbf Z_{ij}&=\mathbf z_{i-1}+h_i\sum_k a_{jk}\mathbf f_{ik},&a_{jk}&=\Omega_k(c_j),\\ \mathbf z_i&=\mathbf z_{i-1}+h_i\sum_k b_k\mathbf f_{ik},&b_k&=\Omega_k(1). \end{aligned}Zij​zi​​=zi−1​+hi​k∑​ajk​fik​,=zi−1​+hi​k∑​bk​fik​,​ajk​bk​​=Ωk​(cj​),=Ωk​(1).​
(13)

These are the Runge-Kutta stage and update equations. For a state-only ODE they are standard RK; for a DAE the algebraic stage equations are additional. A degree-KKK state polynomial is fixed by its initial value and its derivative at KKK distinct points, so this derivative representation is equivalent to the state-coordinate equations when the state interpolation nodes are distinct.

Not every node set is implicit. For one node ccc, a11=ca_{11}=ca11​=c and b1=1b_1=1b1​=1. The choices c=0,1/2,1c=0,1/2,1c=0,1/2,1 give forward Euler, implicit midpoint and backward Euler. Standard Gauss, Radau IIA and Lobatto IIIA are implicit families (the first Lobatto stage is an explicit evaluation). For Lobatto the derivative nodes include zero; do not append a duplicate zero to the K+1K+1K+1-point state formula.

Partition of unity gives stage times. Since ∑kℓˉk=1\sum_k\bar\ell_k=1∑k​ℓˉk​=1, ∑kΩk(τ)=τ\sum_k\Omega_k(\tau)=\tau∑k​Ωk​(τ)=τ. Hence A1=c\mathbf A\mathbf1=\mathbf cA1=c and bT1=1\mathbf b^T\mathbf1=1bT1=1. For dt/dt=1dt/dt=1dt/dt=1 this reproduces tij=ti−1+hicjt_{ij}=t_{i-1}+h_ic_jtij​=ti−1​+hi​cj​ and ti=ti−1+hit_i=t_{i-1}+h_iti​=ti−1​+hi​. With normalized local coordinate, dt/dτ=hidt/d\tau=h_idt/dτ=hi​, not 1. Always use bkb_kbk​ for the endpoint update; the last row of A\mathbf AA equals bT\mathbf b^TbT only when the last node is 1.

Continuity and degree-of-freedom counting¶

The incoming value on element i+1i+1i+1 equals the endpoint reconstructed on element iii:

zi+1,0=zi=∑j=0Kℓj(1)zij=zi−1+hi∑kbkvik.\mathbf z_{i+1,0}=\mathbf z_i=\sum_{j=0}^K\ell_j(1)\mathbf z_{ij} =\mathbf z_{i-1}+h_i\sum_k b_k\mathbf v_{ik}.zi+1,0​=zi​=j=0∑K​ℓj​(1)zij​=zi−1​+hi​k∑​bk​vik​.
(14)

The state remains continuous when its derivative has a finite jump. Right Radau has cK=1c_K=1cK​=1, so its endpoint is the last stage. Gauss-Legendre has cK<1c_K<1cK​<1; it needs the endpoint evaluation, which generally differs from the last stage.

Controls may be piecewise constant and jump at a boundary. Do not impose continuity unless the physical actuator or chosen approximation requires it. Algebraic variables require a separate check. If g(z,y,u,p,t)=0\mathbf g(\mathbf z,\mathbf y,\mathbf u,\mathbf p,t)=0g(z,y,u,p,t)=0 defines a unique regular local branch y=Y(z,u,p,t)\mathbf y=\mathbf Y(\mathbf z,\mathbf u,\mathbf p,t)y=Y(z,u,p,t) and its inputs are continuous, then y\mathbf yy is continuous. Index 1 alone does not ensure this if u\mathbf uu jumps. In z˙=y\dot z=yz˙=y, 0=y−u0=y-u0=y−u, switching uuu from 1 to 2 makes yyy jump while zzz stays continuous. At a discontinuity, distinguish the left and right values at the shared time.

For the common degree-(K−1)(K-1)(K−1) control and algebraic profile representations, use the KKK-node derivative basis:

uiK(τ)=∑j=1Kℓˉj(τ)Uij,yiK(τ)=∑j=1Kℓˉj(τ)Yij.\mathbf u_i^K(\tau)=\sum_{j=1}^K\bar\ell_j(\tau)\mathbf U_{ij},\qquad \mathbf y_i^K(\tau)=\sum_{j=1}^K\bar\ell_j(\tau)\mathbf Y_{ij}.uiK​(τ)=j=1∑K​ℓˉj​(τ)Uij​,yiK​(τ)=j=1∑K​ℓˉj​(τ)Yij​.
(15)

These profiles need not match across elements. A lower-order control parameterization can instead set all Uij\mathbf U_{ij}Uij​ equal on an element. For a regular algebraic branch, an endpoint algebraic value may also be recovered by solving g=0\mathbf g=0g=0 from the endpoint differential state and the appropriate left/right control; this does not justify equating both sides when the control jumps. Nodal bounds on either interpolated profile still need a between-node check.

For one differential state, fixed mesh and prescribed controls/parameters, an expanded derivative transcription has:

QuantityCount
stage states ZijZ_{ij}Zij​NKNKNK
stage derivatives vijv_{ij}vij​NKNKNK
boundary states z0,…,zNz_0,\ldots,z_Nz0​,…,zN​N+1N+1N+1
stage reconstruction equationsNKNKNK
stage ODE equationsNKNKNK
endpoint update equationsNNN

There are N(2K+1)+1N(2K+1)+1N(2K+1)+1 variables and N(2K+1)N(2K+1)N(2K+1) equations before fixing z0z_0z0​. The initial condition removes the remaining degree of freedom. Each regular algebraic stage variable adds a variable and its equation. Free controls, parameters, durations and terminal constraints change the count. Pyomo may eliminate boundary/stage duplicates or use a different derivative representation; its raw counts need not equal this pedagogical expanded formulation. A square count is necessary for a regular simulation, but does not prove independence or numerical accuracy.

A free final time on a fixed domain¶

Let Δt=tf−t0>0\Delta t=t_f-t_0>0Δt=tf​−t0​>0 and σ=(t−t0)/Δt∈[0,1]\sigma=(t-t_0)/\Delta t\in[0,1]σ=(t−t0​)/Δt∈[0,1]. Then

dzdσ=Δt f(z,y,u,p,t0+Δtσ),0=g(z,y,u,p,t0+Δtσ).\frac{d\mathbf z}{d\sigma}=\Delta t\,\mathbf f(\mathbf z,\mathbf y,\mathbf u,\mathbf p,t_0+\Delta t\sigma),\qquad 0=\mathbf g(\mathbf z,\mathbf y,\mathbf u,\mathbf p,t_0+\Delta t\sigma).dσdz​=Δtf(z,y,u,p,t0​+Δtσ),0=g(z,y,u,p,t0​+Δtσ).
(16)

The transformed derivative is with respect to σ\sigmaσ. The duration multiplies every physical-time right-hand side, and any explicit time argument must also be transformed. Minimize t0+Δtt_0+\Delta tt0​+Δt for minimum arrival time with fixed t0t_0t0​. In Biegler’s notation pfp_fpf​ is this duration; the car code calls it tf because t0=0t_0=0t0​=0.

Normalization fixes the domain on which Pyomo creates points; it does not impose a positive duration. Add a physically meaningful lower bound, initialize within the bounds, and use units to check both sides. The car example uses tf >= 0.001 s. For moving normalized mesh fractions ηi>0\eta_i>0ηi​>0, require ∑iηi=1\sum_i\eta_i=1∑i​ηi​=1 and use physical lengths hi=Δtηih_i=\Delta t\eta_ihi​=Δtηi​; do not multiply by the duration twice. Alternatively optimize physical hih_ihi​ with ∑ihi=Δt\sum_i h_i=\Delta t∑i​hi​=Δt.

TaskPyomo object or operationModeling consequence
Fixed normalized domaindae.ContinuousSet(bounds=(0, 1))the set endpoints do not become time decision variables
Derivative w.r.t. that domaindae.DerivativeVar(z, wrt=sigma)write the scaled differential equation explicitly
Finite differencesdae.finite_difference, nfe, schemeinspect which endpoint derivative rows the stencil omits
Orthogonal collocationdae.collocation, nfe, ncp, scheme="LAGRANGE-RADAU" or "LAGRANGE-LEGENDRE"more stages per element or more elements are distinct refinements
One control per elementtransformation’s reduce_collocation_points(..., var=u, ncp=1, contset=sigma)ties within-element control values; it does not make element lengths variables
Explicit mesh locationsContinuousSet(initialize=[...])fixed locations; an NLP cannot move members of the set

Transformation scheme reference¶

TransformationschemeMesh argumentsInterpretation
dae.finite_differenceBACKWARDnfebackward/implicit Euler in time
dae.finite_differenceFORWARDnfeforward/explicit Euler in time
dae.finite_differenceCENTRALnfecentral finite differences; inspect endpoint coverage
dae.collocationLAGRANGE-RADAUnfe, ncpright Radau IIA (default)
dae.collocationLAGRANGE-LEGENDREnfe, ncpGauss-Legendre

Here nfe is the number of finite elements and ncp the stages per element. The finite-difference transformation has no ncp option, and there is no Pyomo Lobatto scheme. These are spatial derivative formulas too; Euler interpretations refer to discretizing time, not to a time integrator created merely by discretizing space.

The official Pyomo.DAE documentation describes these transformations. Read the generated constraints when a derivative appears at an endpoint: declaration alone does not create its defining equation. For boundary-value problems, use the heat-conduction stencil and diagnostics examples. For initialization of a nonlinear process model, see Pyomo.DAE Example: Temperature Control Lab; use a simulated or coarse solution as a starting profile and check structural diagnostics before relying on a solver message.

Node families and endpoint accuracy¶

For Gauss-Legendre, the KKK nodes are the roots of the shifted degree-KKK Legendre polynomial. The corresponding quadrature integrates all degrees through 2K−12K-12K−1. The orthogonality proof and its assumptions are in Numeric Integration for DAEs.

Right Radau adds the endpoint 1 to the roots of a degree-(K−1)(K-1)(K−1) polynomial orthogonal with weight 1−τ1-\tau1−τ. Lobatto adds 0 and 1 to the roots of a degree-(K−2)(K-2)(K−2) polynomial orthogonal with weight τ(1−τ)\tau(1-\tau)τ(1−τ). These are free-node Jacobi constructions, with the fixed endpoints added afterward. Exact symbolic tables and verification are in Collocation Points and Runge-Kutta Coefficients.

For a sufficiently smooth ODE, the standard Gauss, Radau IIA and Lobatto IIIA endpoint orders are 2K2K2K, 2K−12K-12K−1 and 2K−22K-22K−2. An order-ppp method has an unnormalized one-step defect O(hp+1)O(h^{p+1})O(hp+1), or normalized local truncation error O(hp)O(h^p)O(hp). Stage errors and DAE algebraic-variable errors need not have that same order. Quadrature moment tests alone do not prove every nonlinear Runge-Kutta order condition.

Gauss and Radau IIA are A-stable and algebraically stable. Algebraic stability implies AN-stability; the converse applies for distinct abscissas. Radau IIA also has homogeneous stiff decay. A-stability bounds amplification for left-half-plane eigenvalues; it does not ensure accurate transient decay or convergence of the nonlinear stage solve. Gauss large-step oscillations can be reduced by refining the mesh until the transient is resolved. For a very stiff problem, that can require far more elements than a method with stiff decay.

See Biegler, Section 10.2.2, pp. 290–293; Ascher & Petzold, pp. 101–104 and Exercise 4.13, p. 119. See the numerical-integration guide for the formal stability definitions, rather than treating their names as interchangeable.

A practical choice. Start with right Radau for a stiff model when damping fast homogeneous transients matters. For a smooth nonstiff problem, compare Gauss-Legendre: it has one higher endpoint order at the same stage count. That is a reason to measure error and work, not a universal speed ranking. Gauss oscillations can be resolved by sufficiently fine elements. Lobatto is useful for understanding endpoint choices but is not supplied by Pyomo.DAE.

Local equations and sparse structure¶

Order the variables by element. A collocation row involves stages in its own element, the incoming boundary state, that element’s control coefficients, and any shared parameters. Continuity connects neighboring elements. The Jacobian therefore has local blocks and a border for shared parameters or a free final time. It need not be a plain banded matrix. A stage derivative can couple every state component, so a block can itself be dense. Sparse NLP solvers exploit the incidence pattern and compute derivatives of the transcribed equations.

A simultaneous NLP iterate can violate the dynamic equations. At a converged point it satisfies the discrete residual tolerance, which still leaves a discretization error. In a sequential architecture, successful integration supplies a dynamic trajectory for a trial control; it does not automatically enforce path constraints, state bounds or terminal conditions. The architecture comparison is taught in Differential Algebraic Equations (DAEs).

Difficult cases and further reading¶

  • Free element lengths add products of hih_ihi​ with stage derivatives. They let a discontinuity align with an element boundary, but require positive lengths and sensible movement bounds. Inactive pieces can make many meshes nearly equivalent, leaving weak curvature in the mesh variables. See the executed moving-element car example, and Biegler, pp. 296–298.

  • Scale both variables and residuals. A typical-state scale changes z=zref+Szz^\mathbf z=\mathbf z_{\rm ref}+\mathbf S_z\hat{\mathbf z}z=zref​+Sz​z^; a residual scale changes the nonlinear solver’s numerical balance. Preserve units before choosing either. A duration bound is a physical domain constraint, not a substitute for scaling.

  • An index-1 semi-explicit DAE has locally nonsingular ∂g/∂y\partial\mathbf g/\partial\mathbf y∂g/∂y. Higher-index DAEs and active path constraints can require differentiated consistency conditions or index reduction; general smooth-ODE order claims cannot be transferred unchanged. Biegler, Section 10.4.5, pp. 317–322, develops high-index path constraints.

  • Spatial semi-discretization can generate a stiff ODE or DAE. The discretization, boundary equations and constraint index determine which integrator assumptions apply; the fact that the result is finite-dimensional is insufficient. See the heat-conduction guide.
